Mr. Secretary General, Mr. the Vice
President of the General Assembly,
heads of state and government,
excellencies, ambassadors,
ladies and gentlemen, I appear today
before this assembly, representing the
President of the Republic of Colombia,
Aardo de Laspa, who has asked me to be

a message written by him.
From this moment on, what you will hear
are the words of the president of the
Republic of Colombia.
>> I have asked the vice president of the
republic, Jose Manuel Estreo,
to read this message on my behalf.
I have done so because I assured the
Colombian people that I would not leave
the country during the four years of my
term and I am keeping that promise.
47 days ago, a new government took
office in Colombia.
3 days later, at 7:34
a.m., the Earth shook
a 7.4 4 magnitude earthquake struck my
country.
In a matter of seconds, homes,
hospitals, schools, roads, and bridges
had been totally destroyed or severely
damaged.
The Colombian Geological Service
confirmed that this was the strongest
magnitude earthquake recorded in
Colombia so far this century.
Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives.
4,500 were injured and more than 452,000
people were affected.
36,000 homes were totally destroyed.
They represented the life savings assets
of these people.
The government that had barely started
its work was forced to confront one of
the greatest natural disasters in our
recent history.
There was no time to ask whether we were
ready. We had to act and we did so
from the very outset. I gave one
unequivocal instruction.
We had to save human lives.
There was time for everything else.
Appointments to posts could wait.
Meetings could wait. But my fellow
fellow Colombians trapped underneath the
rubble could not.
The government deployed to the affected
areas alongside the security forces,
emergency services, volunteers and
rescue workers. And from the very
beginning, we started receiving the
generous assistance from friendly
countries and international
organizations
such as all of you.
And today from this rostrm I wish to
express the profound and sincere
gratitude of the Colombian people to all
of you.
The earthquake claimed the lives of many
of our fellow Colombians and destroyed
thousands of homes and buildings and
much infrastructure. But it also
reminded us once again of something that
Colombians are very familiar with. We
might fall. We might suffer. We might
weep, but what we cannot and what we do
not know how to do is give up.
But I'm not only going to talk to you
about this tragedy.
I want to refer to what Colombia decided
to do in its aftermath. On the 7th of
August, I took over a country that had
begun to lose something far more
difficult to rebuild than a road or a
building. That is trust.
Trust in the law that should protect our
citizens. Trust that working, studying,
and doing things well are worthwhile.
Trust in a state that lives up to its
duty. No country, no country can prosper
when its people cease to trust in it.
That's why the government that I lead
has tasked itself with
taking up every possible decision to
enable Colombia to believe in itself
again and to ensure that the world can
believe in Colombia again.
And I call that overarching purpose the
Patria Magro, the miracle nation. The
first step is a basic one, restoring
security.
For far too long, Colombians have had to
live alongside situations that no
society should accept as normal.
A rural farmer having to ask permission
from a terrorist group to work on his
land. A shopkeeper having to hand over
part of the fruits of his labor to
extortionists.
A mother increasingly gripped by fear
every time their child goes out to play
in the park.
that is not and it cannot become the
norm. Conse consequently,
from the very beginning of my
government, I gave the security forces
one clear instruction
to regain territorial control to fully
restore the state's authority and to
confront the structures using terrorism.
My government is determined to do away
with euphemisms. Organizations that
murder, that kidnap, that use
explosives, that recruit children, and
that deliberately resort to terror to
subjugate a society are terrorist
groups.
That is what we call them. And we are
facing up to them with the full
legitimate force of the state within the
constitution and within the law.
But there is another reality that is
very often overlooked. The illicit drugs
produced in Colombia
don't end up in Colombia. Drugs
trafficking
is a transnational
criminal enterprise. Its roots cross
borders. Its money moves through
international financial systems. And its
networks operate across numerous
countries.
I will do everything necessary to combat
that scourge. But a transnational threat
requires the international community to
play its part as well. Security, while
essential, is not enough. A territory
that provides no opportunities, remains
vulnerable.
My administration
is therefore also focused on ensuring
that Colombia grows again.
For years, we have discussed how to
better dist distribute what we have.
That is a legitimate necessary
discussion, but it's absolutely not
enough. We also need to ask ourselves
how are we going to produce more?
In the end, governments can't decree
economic growth.
What they have to do is lay the
foundations for it to occur. In our
miracle nation, we want an idea to be
able to become a business, a business to
create jobs and for jobs to become
well-being for our people.
To those of you anywhere else in the
world who are wondering where to invest,
I would like to invite you to look at
Colombia. It's a country with access to
two oceans,
productive land, energy resources,
enormous biodiversity,
an excellent geographical position, and
a government that champions private
enterprise. But above all, look at our
people.
Colombia
does not want to watch the technological
transformation of our time from the
sidelines. We want to be a part of it.
We want to train young people for super
intelligence, for robotics, for data
science, for agro industry, for
engineering, and for the new economy.
Millions of Colombians
are not asking the state to sort out
their lives. They're asking the state to
give them the opportunity to build those
lives. And that is what gives meaning to
what I have called the miracle nation.
This isn't the name of a government, nor
is it a naive promise that our problems
will just disappear. No, that's not it.
This is the country that we're going to
build. It's a country where security
allows us to reclaim the territories
threatened by terrorism, where trust
attracts investment, where investment
creates jobs, and where growth leads to
better living conditions.
It is a school teacher in Mos Bolivar
teaching with the tools of the 21st
century. It is a rural farmer in Ubate
Kundina Mara who can now sew, sell and
prosper thanks to his work. It's uh a
young woman in Pastor Nadinho preparing
to be a part of f the future industries.
This is the miracle nation that we've
already started to build.
I'm well aware that 47 days is far too
little time to change a country, but it
is enough time to change the course of a
country. And I want Colombia to once
again enjoy strong growth. That growth
should lead to a job for a young person,
a home for a family, timely access to
medicines, a harvest that finds a
market, and Colombians who, thanks to
their own efforts and dedication,
can escape poverty.
This is our miracle economy, an economy
that grows so that people can grow with
it.
Our
relationship with the world is also a
part of this purpose. Over the last few
weeks, we have seen this very tangibly
when friendly countries and
international organizations came to our
aid following the earthquake.
This solidarity
makes full sense when it reaches people,
when it solves problems, and when it
produces results.
And it is precisely because I recognize
the value of that corporation that today
I want to speak frankly about the UN.
I've been critical about this of this
organization. I was critical of it
before I became president and it would
be inconsistent to address this assembly
today and conceal my attempt to consil
my convictions. This criticism isn't
born out of whim or hostility towards
the United Nations. It's based in
political, institutional, doctrinal
considerations.
I believe in the UN as an organization
and it is precisely for that reason that
I believe it's legitimate to ask whether
the institutions that we've been
building are effectively responding to
the problems that that it was created to
address. The charter itself is very
clear here. This organization was born
to maintain international peace and
security
to foster friendly relations among
nations and to promote cooperation in
resolving the major common problems.
Eight decades on the question can cannot
be whether those purposes remain valid.
Of course they do. The questions have
completely changed though. Is the UN
fulfilling those purposes with the
effectiveness demanded by today's world?
Are there bureaucratic structures that
have become excessively cumbersome? Are
we dedicating too many resources, too
much energy to administering procedures
and or too little to resolving problems?
Are we measuring our results rigorously
enough?
Another matter that I wish to address is
human rights.
Colombia defends human rights and will
continue to do so. But my country
believes that protecting human rights
loses credibility when it becomes
subjected to political calculation.
I categorically reject
human rights being used as a banner
raised against some and lowered against
others. Nor can human rights become an
instrument rewarding friends, punishing
adversaries, or worse still, remaining
silent in line with the political
circumstances of the time. Our duty is
to prevent politics from weakening the
defense of human rights. If we want the
system to be respected, it needs to be
serious, consistent, and equally
demanding on all of us. My country is
consistent and therefore we want to
ensure that we have a credible defense
of human rights
and in this just as in so many other
areas the United Nations still has some
room for improvement.
In that connection we trust in a
democratic transition in Venezuela, a
swift, safe, farreaching transition.
There's another doctrinal concern that I
wish to raise just as honestly,
globalism.
Allow me to begin by clarifying what I
mean by that. I'm not talking about
international trade or cooperation among
states, nor am I talking about a
humanity that shares common problems and
responsibilities. All of those things
are absolutely necessary. I'm talking
about a concept according to which
nation, sovereignty, distinct
identities, traditions and the values of
peoples are obstacles that gradually
give way to increasing political and
cultural uniformity decided by super
national bodies. I don't share in that
doctrine which I consider perverse and
harmful. For me, multilateralism isn't
about dissolving nations, but rather
about facilitating cooperation among
them.
Loving one's homeland isn't compatible
with respecting others. Defending
history, culture, values, and traditions
doesn't mean disparaging those of
another. International cooperation is
richer when those who sit around this
table know who they are, where they come
from, and
what the people in whose name they speak
represent.
Several of the questions that I've asked
are not unfamiliar to this organization.
The UN80 initiative has placed on the
table issues of duplication,
fragmentation, administrative burden,
and the way mandates function as part of
an effort to make the United Nations
more efficient and more effective.
President, Secretary General, heads of
state and government excellencies,
acknowledging an institution's
imperfections doesn't mean overlooking
its value. But on the contrary, it might
be a way of strengthening it.
It has never been my style to hide
behind political correctness or to tell
my interlocutors what I imagine they
want to hear. I'm not looking to please
anyone, but rather to set out the
position of the Republic of Colombia
respectfully, cordially, and clearly.
No human institution is perfect.
All can be improved, perfected and the
United Nations is no exception. There is
one specific area that Colombia wishes
to reflect on further. That is the
international fight against terrorism.
This organization has done significant
work here. Since 1963, the international
community has developed 19 universal
legal instruments aimed at preventing
different terrorist acts.
However, after decades of discussion,
there is still no legal definition of
terrorism that is universally agreed by
member states. The UN Office of
Counterterrorism itself has recently
flagged that the lack of a universally
agreed definition beggets legal
uncertainty, discrepancies among
national laws, and causes difficulties
in international cooperation. The
Republic of Colombia believes that the
time has come to move ahead.
We need a common international def
definition that is sufficiently clear
and precise, compatible with
international law and fundamental
safeguards, but also
useful enough so that states can
cooperate effectively in combating acts
of terrorism. A serious definition
should avoid two extremes. On the one
hand, a political disagreement being
arbitrarily characterized as terrorism.
And on the other hand, allowing an
organization to hide murders,
kidnappings, bombings, or deliberate
attacks against civilians behind a
political label in order to evade the
legal consequences of its actions.
Terrorism must be condemned regardless
of the perpetrator, where it is
committed, or the cause they invoke. The
United Nations has
repeatedly reaffirmed that terrorism in
all of its forms and manifestations
represents one of the most serious
threats to international peace and
security.
Now,
a better definition is not enough.
States need better tools to combat this
phenomenon.
We need faster mechanisms for exchanging
information and intelligence. We need
better judicial cooperation, effective
tracing, freezing, seizing instruments
um for assets related to terrorist
financing. And we need closer
cooperation to deal with networks that
operate simultaneously across different
countries. Colombia stands ready to
participate actively in that discussion.
My country wants to see United Nations
where the effectiveness is measured less
by the volume of documents it produces
and far more by the results that it
delivers.
A UN that is less inclined to multiply
processes and more determined to
translate international cooperation into
concrete action. That is the sort of
multilateralism that Colombia is ready
to defend. One that respects the
sovereign equality of states, as the
charter itself provides, but one that is
also capable of acting effectively when
threats recognize no borders.
Drugs trafficking, terrorism,
transnational organized crime, and
illicit economies are precisely those
threats.
Specifically,
my government's foreign policy is guided
by national interest, by the defense of
our sovereignty and by the pursuit of
results.
That national interest I referred to
also has a specific objective that is
ensuring the prosperity of our people.
Foreign policy should serve to create
jobs, to attract investment and
technology, to open markets, and to
create opportunities for Colombians.
With that goal in mind, I wish to extend
an invitation to the world. Come to
Colombia.
Invest in Colombia.
Grow and prosper with Colombia. Believe
in Colombia.
I don't promise you a perfect country,
but I can assure you that I am working
tirelessly to build you a nation that is
to build a nation that is safer, more
prosperous, and with more opportunities
for its people. Colombia does not come
before the world today to ask others to
do for us what it is our responsibility
to do for ourselves. rebuilding our
country, restoring security, growing the

and giving opportunities back to
millions of people are first and
foremost responsibilities that fall to
Colombians.
But we also know that no nation can turn
its back on the world. We need partners
and friends with whom we can trade,
invest, exchange knowledge and address
common threats.
That is the Colombia that I present to
you today. A country that is well aware
of its difficulties, but also of its
enormous potential. A country that
doesn't try to hide its problems, but
rather to confront them. A country that
is getting back on its feet and knows
where it wants to go.
To the nations represented here, I
extend my hand respectfully and through
friendship.
Colombia wants to work with you on
everything that we can build together.
I want within a few years
when the world looks again at my
country, I want them to see a nation
that is safer, more prosperous,
more wellrespected, and above all far
more confident in its own abilities.
And if that is the Colombia that the
world sees,
there'll be no need to explain what I
meant when I spoke of the Patria Magro,
the miracle nation. Thank you very much.
